Upper bounds — holds for every total

  • \(\mathrm{R}_0(f) = O\big(\mathrm{R}(f)^2\log \mathrm{R}(f)\big)\)
    KulkarniTal16tight: up to the log factor
    The fine-grained form of the exponent-$2$ cell in the matrix. Improves $\mathrm{R}_0(f)=O(\mathrm{R}(f)^2\log n)$ [Midrijanis05]: the $\log n$ becomes $\log \mathrm{R}$.
  • \(\mathrm{R}_0(f) \le \mathrm{D}(f) \le 27\,\mathrm{R}(f)^3\)
    Nisan91 BdW02
    The bound you get for free; the cubic version is certainly correct.
  • \(\mathrm{R}_0(f) = O\big(\mathrm{EC}(f)^2\big) \text{ and } \mathrm{EC}(f)\le \mathrm{C}(f)\le \mathrm{EC}(f)^2\)
    GJKKLSSV17
    Expectational certificate complexity is the "quadratically tight" handle on $\mathrm{R}_0$; also $\mathrm{FC}(f)\le\mathrm{EC}(f)=O(\mathrm{FC}(f)^{3/2})$.
  • \(\mathrm{C}(f)\le \mathrm{R}_0(f) \le \mathrm{C}(f)^2\)
    GJKKLSSV17
  • \(\mathrm{R}_0(f) = O\big(\mathrm{Q}(f)^2\,\mathrm{Q}_0(f)\log n\big)\)
    Aaronson08
    A genuinely different route, through quantum measures.

Lower bounds / separations — there is a family achieving this

  • \(\mathrm{R}_0(f_n) = \widetilde\Omega\big(\mathrm{R}(f_n)^2\big)\)
    witness: \(g_{\mathrm{ABBLSS}}\) ABBLSS17

Amplification is not what separates these two: $\mathrm{R}_0$ can be quadratically larger than $\mathrm{R}$ because zero error forces the algorithm to certify its answer on every input, and certificates can be large where the bounded-error algorithm only needs to be right on average. For relations (search problems) the two collapse -- see the partial/relational file.

see also: \(\mathrm{EC}(f)\), \(\mathrm{C}(f)\), \(\mathrm{psD}(S)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{0}(f)\) data/relations/01-classical-core.yaml

relation Gap #

Upper bounds — holds for every relation

  • \(\mathrm{R}_0(S) = O(\mathrm{R}(S))\ \text{ for total search problems with verifiable outputs}\)·
    todo: Pin down the exact hypothesis and a citation; the statement is folklore in the TFNP-query literature but the clean form is hypothesis-dependent.
    If a candidate output can be checked with $O(1)$ further queries (as for $\mathrm{SearchCNF}$, where one reads the falsified clause), then repeating a bounded-error algorithm until the check passes turns $\mathrm{R}$ into $\mathrm{R}_0$ at constant expected cost. This is why the Las Vegas / Monte Carlo distinction largely evaporates for search problems. Deliberately recorded without a form:: the hypothesis is a property of the individual problem, not of the relational setting, so the collapse must not be fed to the transitive closure -- every total function is a relation, and \(g_{\mathrm{ABBLSS}}\) already separates $\mathrm{R}_0$ from $\mathrm{R}$ quadratically.

For relations in general the picture is the one inherited from total functions -- $\mathrm{R}_0$ can be quadratically larger than $\mathrm{R}$ (\(g_{\mathrm{ABBLSS}}\)) -- and the collapse above holds only under a verifiability hypothesis on the search problem.

see also: \(\mathrm{R}_{0}(f)\), \(\mathrm{R}_{\varepsilon}(f)\), \(\mathrm{Search}(\varphi)\), Total functions, partial functions, and relations data/relations/06-settings.yaml

up.note: The direction here is worth pausing on, because the obvious guess is backwards. The private-coin game is harder than $\mathrm{R}_0$: it is the one variant of the four that escapes the collapse to $\mathrm{CA}$, and it is not below $\mathrm{D}$ -- $\mathrm{CG}$ can exceed the number of variables. The public-coin argument that does give $\mathrm{CG}^{\mathrm{pub}} = O(\mathrm{R})$ -- both players run one algorithm on a shared random string and guess the step at which their transcripts diverge -- has no private-coin analogue, since with independent coins the two executions no longer track each other. The stated bound is implicit in the expectational-certificate machinery of [GJKKLSSV17] and is recorded as such in [CGLMSG23, Thm 5.10].
